title: Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make Any Transactions
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make Any Transactions
text:
Problem
Visits records each visit (visit_id, customer_id); Transactions records purchases made during visits (transaction_id, visit_id, amount). For each customer, count the visits in which they bought nothing.

title: Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make Any Transactions
text:
Formalisation
Let \(V\) be the visits and \(T\) the transactions, and write \(V_c = \{v \in V \mid v.\mathrm{customer} = c\}\). The quantity we want is
\[
n(c) = \big|\{\, v \in V_c \mid \nexists\, t \in T : t.\mathrm{visit\_id} = v.\mathrm{visit\_id} \,\}\big|,
\]
reported for every customer with \(n(c) > 0\). In SQL the “there is no \(t\)” condition becomes a left join followed by a test for the null padding.

title: Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make Any Transactions
text:
Solution
SELECT v.customer_id, COUNT(*) AS count_no_trans
FROM Visits v
LEFT JOIN Transactions t ON v.visit_id = t.visit_id
WHERE t.transaction_id IS NULL
GROUP BY v.customer_id;

title: Customer Who Visited but Did Not Make Any Transactions
text:
Pitfalls
My first attempt joined the tables the wrong way round and made four further mistakes:

The table you want to keep in full goes on the left. We want visits without transactions, so Visits is the left table. With Transactions on the left, every row already has a visit and the missing ones can never appear.
= 'NULL' compares against the four-letter string “NULL”. And = NULL is never true either; the test is IS NULL.
Filters belong in WHERE, not inside the SELECT list.
It is GROUP BY, at the end, not BY.
COUNT(column) skips NULLs. After the filter, amount is always NULL, so COUNT(amount) returns 0 for every customer. COUNT(*) counts the rows.

title: Confirmation Rate
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Confirmation Rate
text:
Problem
Signups lists every user; Confirmations records each confirmation request with action either 'confirmed' or 'timeout'. A user’s confirmation rate is the number of confirmed requests divided by their total number of requests, or 0 if they made none. Report it for every user, rounded to two decimal places.

title: Confirmation Rate
text:
Formalisation
For a user \(u\) let \(C_u\) be their confirmation requests. The rate is the mean of an indicator function:
\[
\rho(u) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{|C_u|} \displaystyle\sum_{c \in C_u} \mathbf{1}[\,c.\mathrm{action} = \text{confirmed}\,], & C_u \neq \emptyset, \\[2ex]
0, & C_u = \emptyset.
\end{cases}
\]
The left join supplies the second case automatically: a user with no requests gets a single row whose action is NULL, and the indicator maps it to 0.

title: Confirmation Rate
text:
Solution
SELECT s.user_id,
       ROUND(AVG(CASE WHEN c.action = 'confirmed' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END), 2)
         AS confirmation_rate
FROM Signups s
LEFT JOIN Confirmations c ON s.user_id = c.user_id
GROUP BY s.user_id;

title: Confirmation Rate
text:
Pitfalls

Get the ratio the right way up: confirmed ÷ total, not total ÷ confirmed.
A new column is just an expression with an alias. There is no function to define; write the calculation in SELECT and name it with AS.
Use 1.0, not 1. In PostgreSQL and SQL Server, integer ÷ integer truncates.
COUNT(*) vs COUNT(c.action). With a left join, COUNT(*) counts the NULL row of a user with no requests, COUNT(c.action) does not; the SUM(...)/COUNT(...) version can therefore divide by zero. The AVG form avoids the issue.

title: The Number of Employees Which Report to Each Employee
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: The Number of Employees Which Report to Each Employee
text:
Problem
Employees gives each employee’s employee_id, name, age and the id of the manager they reports_to (NULL for nobody). A manager is anyone with at least one direct report. For each manager, report their id and name, the number of direct reports, and the reports’ average age rounded to the nearest integer, ordered by employee_id.

title: The Number of Employees Which Report to Each Employee
text:
Formalisation
Let \(E\) be the table, with tuples \((\mathrm{id}, \mathrm{name}, \mathrm{rep}, \mathrm{age})\). The self-join pairs the table with itself, with \(e\) playing the manager and \(m\) the report:
\[
\sigma_{\,e.\mathrm{id} = m.\mathrm{rep}}(E \times E) = \{(e, m) \in E \times E \mid m.\mathrm{rep} = e.\mathrm{id}\}.
\]
My query writes exactly this: JOIN with no ON is the Cartesian product \(E \times E\), and the WHERE is the selection.
Grouping by the manager gives, for each \(e\), the fibre of their direct reports
\[
R(e) = \{\, m \in E \mid m.\mathrm{rep} = e.\mathrm{id} \,\},
\]
and the output row for \(e\) is
\[
\Big(e.\mathrm{id},\ e.\mathrm{name},\ |R(e)|,\ \Big[\tfrac{1}{|R(e)|} \textstyle\sum_{m \in R(e)} m.\mathrm{age}\Big]\Big),
\]
where \([\,\cdot\,]\) is rounding to the nearest integer. An inner join keeps only pairs that exist, so employees with \(R(e) = \emptyset\) never appear. That is exactly the problem’s definition of a manager, with no extra filter needed.

title: The Number of Employees Which Report to Each Employee
text:
Solution
SELECT e.employee_id, e.name,
  COUNT(*) AS reports_count,
  ROUND(SUM(m.age)/COUNT(*)) AS average_age
FROM Employees e
JOIN Employees m WHERE e.employee_id = m.reports_to
GROUP BY e.employee_id
ORDER BY e.employee_id ASC;
The same query in the conventional form, with the join condition in ON, AVG for the mean, and aliases named after their roles:
SELECT mgr.employee_id, mgr.name,
  COUNT(*) AS reports_count,
  ROUND(AVG(rep.age)) AS average_age
FROM Employees mgr
JOIN Employees rep ON rep.reports_to = mgr.employee_id
GROUP BY mgr.employee_id
ORDER BY mgr.employee_id;

title: The Number of Employees Which Report to Each Employee
text:
Pitfalls

JOIN without ON is a cross join in MySQL. Adding the condition in WHERE turns it into the inner join, so the query is correct. Putting the condition in ON is clearer, and it is required for a LEFT JOIN, where a WHERE condition on the right-hand table would cancel the outer join (see 1251).
Name aliases by role. Here m is the report, not the manager. mgr and rep make it impossible to mix them up.
SUM(age)/COUNT(*) is AVG(age). Both give 38.5 for ages 41 and 36, which rounds to 39.
Rounding depends on the type. The average of integer ages is an exact decimal, and MySQL rounds exact values half away from zero (38.5 → 39). For floating-point values, ROUND follows the C library, which on many systems rounds half to even.
Group by the key, not the name. Selecting e.name while grouping only by e.employee_id is allowed because the name is determined by the primary key. Grouping by name instead would merge two managers who share a name.

title: Replace Employee ID With The Unique Identifier
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Replace Employee ID With The Unique Identifier
text:
Problem
Employees lists each employee’s id and name; EmployeeUNI maps some of those ids to a unique_id. Show every employee’s name with their unique_id, or NULL if they don’t have one.

title: Replace Employee ID With The Unique Identifier
text:
Formalisation
Write \(E\) for Employees and \(U\) for EmployeeUNI, and let \(\theta(e,u)\) be the condition \(e.\mathrm{id} = u.\mathrm{id}\). An inner join is a filtered Cartesian product,
\[
E \bowtie_\theta U = \sigma_\theta(E \times U) = \{(e,u) \in E \times U \mid \theta(e,u)\},
\]
and the left join, written here \(\bowtie^{\mathrm{L}}\), adds back every employee that matched nothing, paired with a row of nulls:
\[
E \mathbin{\bowtie^{\mathrm{L}}_\theta} U = \sigma_\theta(E \times U) \;\cup\; \{(e, \mathrm{NULL}) \mid e \in E,\ \nexists\, u \in U : \theta(e,u)\}.
\]
The answer is the projection of this onto \((u.\texttt{unique\_id},\ e.\texttt{name})\).

title: Replace Employee ID With The Unique Identifier
text:
Solution
SELECT u.unique_id, e.name
FROM Employees e
LEFT JOIN EmployeeUNI u ON e.id = u.id;

title: Replace Employee ID With The Unique Identifier
text:
Pitfalls

“Show NULL if missing” means LEFT JOIN. A plain JOIN drops employees without a unique id.
ON pairs rows; it does not remove left-hand rows. To drop rows you need a WHERE, e.g. WHERE u.id IS NULL keeps only the unmatched employees (the anti-join, see 1581).
Aliases are bound variables. e and u range over the rows of each table; the letters are arbitrary, but once a table is aliased you must use the alias.

title: Product Sales Analysis I
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Product Sales Analysis I
text:
Problem
Sales records each sale (sale_id, product_id, year, quantity, price); Product maps product_id to product_name. For every sale, report the product name, year and price.

title: Product Sales Analysis I
text:
Formalisation
With \(S\) for Sales and \(P\) for Product, pair each sale with its product and project:
\[
\pi_{\,p.\mathrm{name},\ s.\mathrm{year},\ s.\mathrm{price}}\Big(\{(s,p) \in S \times P \mid s.\mathrm{product\_id} = p.\mathrm{product\_id}\}\Big).
\]
Since product_id is the key of Product, each sale matches exactly one product, so there is one output row per sale.

title: Product Sales Analysis I
text:
Solution
SELECT p.product_name, s.year, s.price
FROM Sales s
JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = s.product_id;
If you do want a named intermediate result, the syntax is a common table expression, written before the query that uses it:
WITH Output AS (
    SELECT p.product_name, s.year, s.price
    FROM Sales s
    JOIN Product p ON p.product_id = s.product_id
)
SELECT product_name, year, price FROM Output;

title: Product Sales Analysis I
text:
Pitfalls

AS name after a query is not valid. A query is named with WITH name AS (...), or as a subquery FROM (SELECT ...) AS name.
SELECT * inside a CTE can fail. Both tables have a product_id column, so the CTE would have two columns with the same name (“Duplicate column name”).
Two statements need a ; between them.
SQL is not executed in the order it is written. The logical order is FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY, which is why aliases defined in FROM can be used in SELECT.

title: Recyclable and Low Fat Products
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Recyclable and Low Fat Products
text:
Problem
A Products table records, for each product_id, whether the product is low fat and whether it is recyclable (each 'Y' or 'N'). Return the ids of products that are both.

title: Recyclable and Low Fat Products
text:
Formalisation
Let the table be the (multi)set
\[
P \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times \{Y,N\} \times \{Y,N\}, \qquad (i, f, r) = (\texttt{product\_id}, \texttt{low\_fats}, \texttt{recyclable}),
\]
then the task is to first introduce the selection
\[
\sigma_{f=Y \wedge r=Y}(P) = \{(i,f,r) \in P \mid f = Y \wedge r = Y\}.
\]
Since we only want the product_id, we take the image of this set under the projection \(\pi_i : (i,f,r) \mapsto i\):
\[
\pi_i\big(\sigma_{f=Y \wedge r=Y}(P)\big) = \{\, i \mid (i, Y, Y) \in P \,\}.
\]
Because product_id is the primary key, each \(i\) appears in exactly one tuple, so \(P\) is a genuine set (the graph of a function \(g : I \to \{Y,N\}^2\)) and the answer is the preimage \(g^{-1}(\{(Y,Y)\})\). The projection cannot produce duplicates.

title: Recyclable and Low Fat Products
text:
Solution
SELECT product_id
FROM Products
WHERE low_fats = 'Y' AND recyclable = 'Y';

title: Recyclable and Low Fat Products
text:
Pitfalls

''Y'' is not 'Y'. Two single quotes inside a string are an escaped literal quote.
IF() returns a value; it does not filter. IF(cond, a, b) produces a column for every row. Keeping only some rows is the job of WHERE.
Combine conditions with AND, not a comma. A comma in the SELECT list separates columns.
The values are strings. The columns are ENUM('Y','N'), so test = 'Y'; they are not booleans.

title: About Me
text:
Hi, I’m Dylan. I’m a theoretical physics graduate from the University of Cambridge. This is my space to write freely about anything that has been lingering in my mind. I will mainly be writing about aspects of theoretical and mathematical physics that I enjoy and believe deserve more attention.
I will try to keep the explanations accessible and build up any required mathematics from undergraduate-level arguments. This does not mean that you need to be a mathematician to enjoy these articles. Geometric and visual arguments will also be employed liberally because of their beauty and physical intuition.
Anyway, I hope you can learn some cool physics and maths from this page! Please note that any views expressed here are my own.

title: Curvature, Curvature, Curvature!
Curvature, Curvature, Curvature!
Curvature, Curvature, Curvature!
text:
Curvature and Physics
Given the lengthy introduction above to the numerous types of curvature, I will now give a view of why it is useful and necessary in phyiscs. I also want to try and convince you of the theoretical power of geometry in physics.

Geometry and Gravity
You are probably familiar with the idea that gravity is a force. This is the Newtonian picture of gravity, which is very useful for many applications. However, it is not the most fundamental description of gravity. The more fundamental description is given by Einstein’s General Theory of Relativity, which describes gravity as a manifestation of the curvature of spacetime.
The language of this is differential geometry, which we have been developing. The idea is that massive objects cause spacetime to curve, and this curvature affects the motion of objects. In this picture, what we perceive as the force of gravity is actually the result of objects following geodesics in curved spacetime. So, in that sense gravity isn’t really a force at all, but rather a manifestation of the geometry of spacetime. Spacetime is a four-dimensional manifold, with three spatial dimensions and one time dimension. The curvature of spacetime is described by the Riemann curvature tensor, which we have discussed above. The Einstein field equations relate the curvature of spacetime to the distribution of matter and energy, and they are given by
\[\begin{equation}
R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}R+\Lambda g_{\mu\nu}=\frac{8\pi G}{c^4}T_{\mu\nu} \, ,
\end{equation}\]
where \(T_{\mu \nu}\) is the energy-momentum tensor, \(G\) is the gravitational constant, \(c\) is the speed of light, and \(\Lambda\) is the cosmological constant. The left-hand side of the equation describes the curvature of spacetime, while the right-hand side describes the distribution of matter and energy. The Einstein field equations are a set of ten interrelated differential equations that describe how matter and energy influence the curvature of spacetime, and they form the foundation of our understanding of gravity in the context of general relativity. As a simple example, consider the case where we have no matter in our universe and no cosmological constant, so that \(T_{\mu\nu}=0\) and \(\Lambda = 0\). In this case, the Einstein field equations reduce to
\[\begin{equation}
R_{\mu\nu}-\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}R = 0 \, .
\end{equation}\]
We can take the trace of this equation by contracting with the inverse metric \(g^{\mu\nu}\), which gives
\[\begin{equation}
R-\frac{1}{2}g^{\mu \nu}g_{\mu\nu}R =0 \, .
\end{equation}\]
Using the relation \(g_{\mu\nu}g^{\mu\nu}=4\) in four dimensions, we can simplify this to
\[\begin{equation}
-R = 0 \, ,
\end{equation}\] so the Ricci scalar vanishes. Substituting this back into the field equations leaves \(R_{\mu\nu}=0\), which means the spacetime is Ricci flat. This is a simple example of how the Einstein field equations relate the curvature of spacetime to the distribution of matter and energy. I should be careful here though: Ricci flat does not mean flat. Recall that the Ricci tensor only records the trace of the Riemann tensor (the net focusing of a bundle of geodesics). The remaining trace-free part, called the Weyl tensor, is free to be non-zero even in empty space. This is how tidal forces and gravitational waves can exist where there is no matter at all. Flat Minkowski space is the simplest vacuum solution, but it is far from the only one.
The simplest, non-trivial solution to the Einstein field equations is the Schwarzschild solution, which describes the spacetime geometry outside a spherically symmetric, non-rotating mass. The Schwarzschild metric is given by \[\begin{equation}
ds^2 = -\left(1-\frac{2GM}{c^2r}\right)c^2dt^2 + \left(1-\frac{2GM}{c^2r}\right)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta d\phi^2) \, ,
\end{equation}\] where \(M\) is the mass of the object, and \((t,r,\theta,\phi)\) are the Schwarzschild coordinates. This is a vacuum solution, so its Ricci tensor vanishes everywhere outside the mass. Its Riemann tensor, however, does not. A convenient check is the Kretschmann scalar,
\[\begin{equation}
R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} = \frac{48G^2M^2}{c^4r^6} \, ,
\end{equation}\]
which is clearly non-zero, so the spacetime is indeed curved (and genuinely singular at \(r=0\)). The Schwarzschild solution has been extensively tested and confirmed through observations, such as the bending of light around massive objects (gravitational lensing) and the precession of planetary orbits.


Geometry and Gauge Theories
The standard model of particle physics is a gauge theory, which describes the fundamental forces of nature (except for gravity) in terms of symmetries and fields. In this framework, the interactions between particles are mediated by gauge bosons, which are associated with the symmetries of the theory. The mathematical structure of gauge theories is deeply connected to differential geometry, as the gauge fields can be interpreted as ``connections on principal bundles’’, and the field strengths correspond to curvature forms. I won’t be super rigorous here, but the idea is that the gauge fields can be thought of as providing a way to compare vectors in different tangent spaces, similar to how the Levi-Civita connection allows us to compare vectors in different tangent spaces on a manifold. In this sense they are themselves connections of the theory. The curvature of the gauge fields then encodes information about the interactions between particles, and the dynamics of the gauge fields are governed by equations that are analogous to the Einstein field equations in general relativity.
Let’s see this in a bit more detail. Consider a gauge theory with a gauge group \(G\), which is a Lie group that describes the symmetries of the theory. The gauge fields are represented by a connection \(A\), which is a Lie algebra-valued one-form on spacetime. The field strength \(F\) is then given by the curvature of the connection, which can be expressed as \[\begin{equation}
F = dA + A \wedge A \, ,
\end{equation}\] where \(d\) is the exterior derivative and \(\wedge\) is the wedge product. The field strength \(F\) encodes the information about the interactions between particles, and it satisfies the Bianchi identity, which is a generalization of the second Bianchi identity we discussed earlier. The dynamics of the gauge fields are governed by the Yang-Mills equations, which are analogous to the Einstein field equations in general relativity. The Yang-Mills equations can be derived from an action principle, and they describe how the gauge fields evolve in response to the presence of matter and other gauge fields. The curvature of the gauge fields plays a central role in determining the behavior of particles and their interactions, and it is intimately connected to the symmetries of the theory. In this way, differential geometry provides a powerful framework for understanding the fundamental forces of nature and the interactions between particles in the context of gauge theories.
The easiest one we can look at is the \(U(1)\) gauge theory, which describes electromagnetism. In this case, the gauge group is \(U(1)\), and the gauge field \(A\) corresponds to the electromagnetic potential. The field strength \(F\) is then given by \[\begin{equation}
F = dA = \frac{1}{2}(\partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu) \, \text{d}x^\mu \wedge \text{d}x^\nu \, ,
\end{equation}\] which is the familiar electromagnetic field tensor given by the matrix \[\begin{equation}
F_{\mu \nu} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -E_x & -E_y & -E_z \\
E_x & 0 & -B_z & B_y \\
E_y & B_z & 0 & -B_x \\
E_z & -B_y & B_x & 0
\end{pmatrix} \, .
\end{equation}\] The Bianchi identity in this case reduces to the statement \[\begin{equation}dF = 0 \, ,
\end{equation}\] which corresponds to the homogeneous Maxwell equations. The dynamics of the electromagnetic field are governed by the inhomogeneous Maxwell equations, which can be derived from the action principle and are given by \[\begin{equation}
d*F = *J \, ,
\end{equation}\] where \(*\) is the Hodge star operator and \(J\) is the current one-form (up to a sign that depends on your conventions).


Geometry and Beyond the Standard Model Physics
So we now have two theories, both built on curvature. General relativity describes gravity through the curvature of the Levi-Civita connection, and the standard model describes the other three forces through the curvature of gauge connections. Between them they describe essentially every experiment we have ever done. However, the standard model is not the end of the story. It says nothing about gravity at the quantum level, it contains nothing that could be dark matter, in its original form it gives neutrinos no mass (they have one), and it has around nineteen free parameters which we simply have to measure and put in by hand. It also offers no explanation for why matter comes in exactly three copies, or generations, of quarks and leptons.
Attempts to fix these problems get lumped together under the name beyond the standard model (BSM) physics. There are far too many proposals to cover here, and most of them are yet to be tested. Instead, I want to convince you that a surprising number of the best ideas are geometric at heart, and that the curvature we spent so long building up above is doing most of the heavy lifting.

The Same Commutator, Twice
Before going beyond anything, I want to make the link between the last two sections explicit, since it is really the thread running through this entire post. Recall that for the Levi-Civita connection in a coordinate basis, the Riemann tensor came from the commutator of two covariant derivatives. Acting on the components of a vector field this reads
\[\begin{equation}
\left[\nabla_\mu,\nabla_\nu\right]V^\rho = R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}V^\sigma \, .
\end{equation}\]
Now take a matter field \(\psi\), say an electron or a quark, which transforms under some gauge group \(G\). At each point of spacetime \(\psi(x)\) is a vector, but it lives in an internal vector space attached to that point rather than in the tangent space. For a quark, this is the three-dimensional space of colours. Just as before, there is no canonical way to compare \(\psi\) at two different points, so we need a connection. This is precisely the job of the gauge field, and the gauge covariant derivative is
\[\begin{equation}
D_\mu\psi = \partial_\mu\psi + A_\mu\psi \, ,
\end{equation}\]
where \(A_\mu\) is a matrix in the Lie algebra of \(G\) (I have absorbed the coupling constant and a factor of \(i\) into \(A\) to keep things tidy). Compare this to \(\nabla_\mu V^\rho = \partial_\mu V^\rho + \Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\sigma}V^\sigma\). The gauge field is playing exactly the role of the Christoffel symbols. Let’s take the commutator,
\[\begin{align}
\left[D_\mu,D_\nu\right]\psi
&= \partial_\mu\partial_\nu\psi + (\partial_\mu A_\nu)\psi + A_\nu\partial_\mu\psi + A_\mu\partial_\nu\psi + A_\mu A_\nu\psi - (\mu\leftrightarrow\nu) \\
&= \left(\partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu + \left[A_\mu,A_\nu\right]\right)\psi \\
&= F_{\mu\nu}\psi \, .
\end{align}\]
The second derivatives cancel because partial derivatives commute, and the \(A\,\partial\psi\) terms cancel because they are symmetric in \(\mu\) and \(\nu\). What is left over are exactly the components of \(F = \mathrm{d}A + A\wedge A\) from earlier. So the field strength is the failure of gauge covariant derivatives to commute, in exactly the same way that the Riemann tensor is the failure of ordinary covariant derivatives to commute.
The analogy goes further. Under a gauge transformation \(\psi \rightarrow g(x)\psi\), the gauge field transforms as
\[\begin{equation}
A_\mu \rightarrow gA_\mu g^{-1} - (\partial_\mu g)g^{-1} \, ,
\end{equation}\]
which is not very nice at all because of the derivative term. This is the same disease the Christoffel symbols have: they are not tensors, and in Riemann normal coordinates we can even make them vanish at a point. Their curvature, however, behaves beautifully,
\[\begin{equation}
F_{\mu\nu} \rightarrow gF_{\mu\nu}g^{-1} \, ,
\end{equation}\]
so gauge invariant quantities, like \(\operatorname{tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})\), are built out of curvature. This is the point I made right back at the start when discussing parameterisation invariance: the labels we choose are bookkeeping, and curvature is the thing that survives. We can collect the whole dictionary into a table.







General relativity
Gauge theory




Tangent space \(T_pM\)
Internal space at \(p\) (e.g. colour space)


Change of frame
Gauge transformation \(g(x)\)


Christoffel symbols \(\Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\sigma}\)
Gauge field \(A_\mu\)


Covariant derivative \(\nabla_\mu\)
Gauge covariant derivative \(D_\mu\)


Riemann tensor \(R^\rho{}_{\sigma\mu\nu}\)
Field strength \(F_{\mu\nu}\)


Parallel transport
Wilson line \(\mathcal{P}\exp\left(-\int_\gamma A\right)\)


Second Bianchi identity
\(DF = 0\)



To be completely honest, the gravitational partner of \(A_\mu\) is really the spin connection (the Christoffel symbols written in an orthonormal frame), but the idea is identical. The Wilson line is just the solution to \(D_t\psi = 0\) along a curve, i.e. parallel transport for \(\psi\), and the \(\mathcal{P}\) means the matrices are ordered along the path. Around a tiny closed loop it differs from the identity by \(F_{\mu\nu}\) times the area of the loop, exactly as a vector carried around a small loop on a curved surface comes back rotated by an amount set by the Riemann tensor.
There is one important place where the analogy breaks, however, and it matters a great deal. The Yang-Mills action is quadratic in curvature, \(S_{\text{YM}} \propto \int \operatorname{tr}(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu})\,\mathrm{d}^4x\), while the Einstein-Hilbert action of general relativity,
\[\begin{equation}
S_{\text{EH}} = \frac{c^4}{16\pi G}\int R\,\sqrt{-g}\,\mathrm{d}^4x \, ,
\end{equation}\]
is linear in curvature, and its connection is not an independent field but is built out of the metric. One consequence is that Newton’s constant has dimensions (in natural units it is an inverse mass squared), and when we try to quantise gravity like the other forces we get a theory which is non-renormalisable. This is the deepest reason we need to go beyond the standard model, and it is why so many of the ideas below are really attempts to put gravity and gauge theory on the same geometric footing.


Bigger Connections: Grand Unification
The first BSM idea is visible from the dictionary alone. The gauge group of the standard model is
\[\begin{equation}
G_{\text{SM}} = SU(3)\times SU(2)\times U(1) \, ,
\end{equation}\]
which means three separate connections, three separate curvatures, and three separate coupling constants. That is rather untidy. A Grand Unified Theory (GUT) proposes that they are all pieces of a single connection for a bigger group. The original example is \(SU(5)\), due to Georgi and Glashow in 1974. Its Lie algebra is 24-dimensional, and it decomposes as
\[\begin{equation}
\mathbf{24} = \underbrace{(\mathbf{8},\mathbf{1})}_{\text{gluons}} \oplus \underbrace{(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{3})\oplus(\mathbf{1},\mathbf{1})}_{W^\pm,\,Z,\,\gamma} \oplus \underbrace{(\mathbf{3},\mathbf{2})\oplus(\bar{\mathbf{3}},\mathbf{2})}_{12 \text{ new bosons}} \, .
\end{equation}\]
Geometrically, the single field strength \(F\) of \(SU(5)\) is a \(5\times5\) matrix, and the gluons, weak bosons and photon sit in blocks of it. The off-diagonal blocks contain twelve new, extremely heavy gauge bosons which can turn quarks into leptons. This predicts that the proton is unstable. Sadly (or happily, depending on how attached you are to your atoms) proton decay has never been seen, and experiments now tell us the proton lives for more than \(10^{34}\) years. This rules out the simplest \(SU(5)\) model, but not the idea of unification itself, and larger groups like \(SO(10)\) remain very much alive. We will meet another prediction of GUTs, magnetic monopoles, shortly.


Kaluza-Klein: Electromagnetism from a Fifth Dimension
The dictionary is very suggestive, but general relativity and gauge theory are still two separate theories glued together. Could the gauge connection literally be part of the geometry of spacetime? Remarkably, Theodor Kaluza wrote to Einstein with exactly this idea in 1919, only a few years after general relativity itself, and Oskar Klein refined it in 1926.
Suppose spacetime has five dimensions, with the fifth coordinate \(y\) curled up into a small circle of radius \(L\), so that \(y \sim y + 2\pi L\). If nothing depends on \(y\), the most general metric we can write down is
\[\begin{equation}
\mathrm{d}s^2 = g_{\mu\nu}(x)\,\mathrm{d}x^\mu\mathrm{d}x^\nu + \phi(x)^2\left(\mathrm{d}y + A_\mu(x)\,\mathrm{d}x^\mu\right)^2 \, .
\end{equation}\]
A five-dimensional metric has 15 independent components, and these have split up into \(10\) for the four-dimensional metric \(g_{\mu\nu}\), \(4\) for a vector \(A_\mu\), and \(1\) for a scalar \(\phi\). Now, why should \(A_\mu\) be the electromagnetic potential? Let’s do the same sort of relabelling we did with our curves at the very beginning, and shift the coordinate on the circle by an amount that depends on where we are in spacetime,
\[\begin{equation}
y \rightarrow y + \lambda(x) \, .
\end{equation}\]
This is just a diffeomorphism of the five-dimensional spacetime, so it cannot change any physics. Since \(\mathrm{d}y \rightarrow \mathrm{d}y + \partial_\mu\lambda\,\mathrm{d}x^\mu\), the metric keeps exactly the same form provided
\[\begin{equation}
A_\mu \rightarrow A_\mu - \partial_\mu\lambda \, ,
\end{equation}\]
which is precisely a \(U(1)\) gauge transformation. So gauge invariance in four dimensions is nothing more than diffeomorphism invariance in five, and the gauge group \(U(1)\) is just the group of rotations of the circle. I find this genuinely beautiful.
It gets better. If you compute the Ricci scalar of the five-dimensional metric (one of those calculations every physicist should do once and then never again) you find
\[\begin{equation}
R^{(5)} = R^{(4)} - \frac{1}{4}\phi^2F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu} - \frac{2}{\phi}\Box\phi \, .
\end{equation}\]
Using \(\sqrt{-G} = \phi\sqrt{-g}\) for the five-dimensional volume factor and integrating over the circle, the five-dimensional Einstein-Hilbert action becomes (in units with \(\hbar = c = 1\))
\[\begin{equation}
\frac{1}{16\pi G_5}\int \mathrm{d}^5x\,\sqrt{-G}\,R^{(5)}
= \frac{2\pi L}{16\pi G_5}\int \mathrm{d}^4x\,\sqrt{-g}\left(\phi R^{(4)} - \frac{1}{4}\phi^3F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}\right) \, ,
\end{equation}\]
where the \(\Box\phi\) term has become a total derivative and dropped out. If we freeze \(\phi = 1\), this is exactly the Einstein-Hilbert action plus the Maxwell action, with the four-dimensional Newton constant \(G_4 = G_5/2\pi L\). Five-dimensional gravity with no matter at all has produced four-dimensional gravity and electromagnetism. The electromagnetic field strength is literally a component of the curvature of a higher dimensional spacetime.
There is also a lovely explanation of why electric charge is quantised. Any field on this spacetime can be Fourier expanded around the circle,
\[\begin{equation}
\Phi(x,y) = \sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\varphi_n(x)\,e^{iny/L} \, .
\end{equation}\]
Under \(y\rightarrow y+\lambda(x)\), the mode \(\varphi_n\) picks up the phase \(e^{in\lambda/L}\), so it has \(U(1)\) charge proportional to \(n\). Charge is simply momentum around the circle, and because the circle is compact, momentum comes in discrete lumps. After normalising \(A_\mu\) properly, the charge and mass of the \(n\)-th mode are
\[\begin{align}
q_n &= \frac{n\sqrt{16\pi G_4}}{L} \, , & m_n &= \frac{|n|}{L} \, .
\end{align}\]
Setting \(q_1\) equal to the charge of the electron gives a radius of roughly \(10^{-34}\,\)m, which explains why we have never noticed the fifth dimension. Unfortunately, it also gives a mass of around \(10^{17}\,\)GeV for the first charged particle, while the electron weighs about \(5\times10^{-4}\,\)GeV. So the simplest version of the theory cannot be right as it stands. There are other problems too. The scalar \(\phi\) cannot actually be frozen consistently (its equation of motion would then force \(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}=0\)), so it is a new field whose dynamics must be dealt with. Worse, Witten showed that compactifications like this struggle to produce the chiral fermions of the standard model, in which left and right-handed particles feel the weak force differently.
Nevertheless the idea refused to die. To get a non-abelian gauge group, we replace the circle with a compact internal manifold whose symmetries form that group. Witten worked out in 1981 that the smallest internal manifold with symmetry group \(SU(3)\times SU(2)\times U(1)\) has seven dimensions, giving eleven in total. Coincidentally (or perhaps not), eleven is also the maximum dimension in which supergravity can be formulated, and the dimension of what we now call M-theory. More modern versions, such as the large extra dimensions of Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos and Dvali, or the warped extra dimension of Randall and Sundrum, use the geometry of extra dimensions to try to explain why gravity is so much weaker than the other forces. These predict towers of Kaluza-Klein particles, which have been searched for at the LHC (so far without success).


Curvature That Counts: Topology
I now want to return to Gauss, because one of his results turns out to be lurking behind some of the most important ideas in BSM physics. For a closed, orientable surface \(M\) (one with no boundary, like a sphere or a doughnut), the Gauss-Bonnet theorem states that
\[\begin{equation}
\int_M K\,\mathrm{d}A = 2\pi\chi(M) \, , \qquad \chi(M) = 2 - 2\mathfrak{g} \, ,
\end{equation}\]
where \(K\) is the Gaussian curvature from before, \(\chi(M)\) is the Euler characteristic, and \(\mathfrak{g}\) is the number of holes (the genus). As a quick check, a sphere of radius \(r\) has \(K = 1/r^2\) everywhere and area \(4\pi r^2\), so the left-hand side is \(4\pi\), while a sphere has no holes and \(\chi = 2\).
This theorem is far stranger than it looks. If I squash my sphere into an egg, or a potato, the Gaussian curvature changes from point to point in a complicated way, but its integral cannot change at all. The left-hand side is built from local geometry, while the right-hand side is an integer that only knows about the global shape. Since a continuous deformation cannot make an integer jump, the integral of curvature is topological. This exact pattern, an integral of curvature that can only take quantised values, appears all over the place in gauge theory.
Magnetic monopoles. The simplest example is the \(U(1)\) gauge theory of electromagnetism, where the curvature is \(F = \mathrm{d}A\). The total magnetic flux through a closed surface is \(\int_{S^2}F\), and if this surface encloses a magnetic monopole, the flux is non-zero. Dirac showed in 1931 that for quantum mechanics to be consistent, an electric charge \(e\) must satisfy (with \(\hbar=1\))
\[\begin{equation}
\frac{e}{2\pi}\int_{S^2}F \in \mathbb{Z} \, .
\end{equation}\]
The left-hand side is called the first Chern number, and it is the gauge theory cousin of Gauss-Bonnet. Its physical consequence is striking: if a single magnetic monopole exists anywhere in the universe, every electric charge must be quantised. Monopoles do not exist in the standard model, but they are an unavoidable prediction of every GUT, as shown by ’t Hooft and Polyakov in 1974, with masses of around \(10^{16}\) to \(10^{17}\,\)GeV. None have ever been found, and explaining why there are so few of them was one of the original motivations for cosmic inflation.
Instantons and the strong CP problem. In four dimensions, the analogous topological integral for a non-abelian gauge field is
\[\begin{equation}
k = \frac{1}{8\pi^2}\int \operatorname{tr}\left(F\wedge F\right) \in \mathbb{Z} \, ,
\end{equation}\]
the second Chern number, sometimes called the instanton number (I am working in Euclidean signature, with spacetime compactified to a four-sphere, and ignoring the sign conventions that plague this subject). Gauge field configurations with \(k\neq0\) are called instantons. You can check, using \(F = \mathrm{d}A + A\wedge A\) and the cyclicity of the trace, that
\[\begin{equation}
\operatorname{tr}\left(F\wedge F\right) = \mathrm{d}\operatorname{tr}\left(A\wedge\mathrm{d}A + \frac{2}{3}A\wedge A\wedge A\right) \, ,
\end{equation}\]
so \(\operatorname{tr}(F\wedge F)\) is a total derivative, which is why its integral only cares about topology. This means that nothing stops us from adding a term like
\[\begin{equation}
S_\theta = \frac{\theta}{8\pi^2}\int\operatorname{tr}\left(F\wedge F\right)
\end{equation}\]
to the action of QCD. It does not change the classical equations of motion at all, but in the quantum theory each topological sector is weighted by \(e^{i\theta k}\), so \(\theta\) is an angle and it has real physical effects. For electromagnetism, \(F\wedge F\) is proportional to \(\mathbf{E}\cdot\mathbf{B}\), which changes sign under parity and under time reversal. So a non-zero \(\theta\) violates CP symmetry, and in particular it would give the neutron an electric dipole moment. A natural value of \(\theta\) would be of order one, but experiments tell us that \(|\theta| \lesssim 10^{-10}\) (strictly speaking, the bound is on a combination of \(\theta\) and the phases of the quark masses).
Why should an angle, which could be anything, be so absurdly close to zero? This is the strong CP problem. The most popular solution, due to Peccei and Quinn in 1977, is to promote \(\theta\) to a dynamical field, \(\theta \rightarrow a(x)/f_a\). Instanton effects then generate a potential for \(a(x)\) whose minimum sits exactly where the effective \(\theta\) vanishes, so the universe relaxes to \(\theta = 0\) on its own. Weinberg and Wilczek pointed out that this new field is a particle, the axion. It is very light and interacts very weakly, which makes it one of the leading candidates for dark matter, and there are experiments searching for it right now. So an integral of curvature that cannot even be seen in the classical equations of motion has led to one of the most promising pieces of BSM physics.


Holonomy and the Shape of Hidden Dimensions
We have seen that extra dimensions can hide, so long as they are small. String theory goes further and requires them: the superstring is only consistent in ten dimensions, so six of them must be curled up into some compact manifold \(X\). The obvious question is which one, and the answer is controlled by an object we have already met in disguise.
Recall that when we parallel transport a vector around a closed loop it generally comes back changed. Let’s fix a point \(p\) and collect together the parallel transport maps \(P_\gamma\) around every loop \(\gamma\) based at \(p\). These maps can be composed (go around one loop then the other) and inverted (go around the loop backwards), so they form a group, called the holonomy group,
\[\begin{equation}
\operatorname{Hol}_p(\nabla) = \left\{P_\gamma : \gamma \text{ a loop at } p\right\} \, .
\end{equation}\]
Since we showed that parallel transport preserves lengths and angles, every \(P_\gamma\) is a rotation (or reflection), so for an \(n\)-dimensional manifold the holonomy group sits inside \(O(n)\). On a flat torus, every vector comes back unchanged and the holonomy is trivial. On a sphere, a vector carried around a loop comes back rotated by an angle equal to \(\int K\,\mathrm{d}A\) over the region the loop encloses (Gauss-Bonnet again!), so the holonomy is the full rotation group \(SO(2)\). In general, for small loops the holonomy is generated by the Riemann tensor, so holonomy is really the global version of curvature.
For a generic oriented six-dimensional manifold the holonomy group is \(SO(6)\). However, if we want the four-dimensional world to have supersymmetry, which is itself a BSM proposal that helps with the large gap between the weak scale and the Planck scale, it turns out we need a spinor \(\eta\) on \(X\) that is covariantly constant,
\[\begin{equation}
\nabla_m\eta = 0 \, .
\end{equation}\]
Here is where our commutator comes back one final time. If \(\nabla_m\eta=0\) then certainly \([\nabla_m,\nabla_n]\eta = 0\). For spinors, the commutator of covariant derivatives is
\[\begin{equation}
\left[\nabla_m,\nabla_n\right]\eta = \frac{1}{4}R_{mnab}\gamma^{ab}\eta \, ,
\end{equation}\]
where the \(\gamma^a\) are the gamma matrices and \(\gamma^{ab} = \frac{1}{2}[\gamma^a,\gamma^b]\). Multiplying by \(\gamma^n\) and using the first Bianchi identity to kill one of the terms, you can show that this forces
\[\begin{equation}
R_{mn}\gamma^n\eta = 0 \, .
\end{equation}\]
Fix \(m\) and let \(v^n = R_m{}^n\). Multiplying by \(v^p\gamma_p\) and using \(\{\gamma^a,\gamma^b\} = 2g^{ab}\) gives \(v_nv^n\eta = 0\), and since the metric is positive definite and \(\eta\neq0\), we must have \(v=0\). Therefore
\[\begin{equation}
R_{mn} = 0 \, .
\end{equation}\]
The internal space must be Ricci flat, which is exactly the vacuum Einstein equation we met in the gravity section! At the same time, the holonomy must preserve \(\eta\). In six dimensions spinors transform as the \(\mathbf{4}\) of \(SU(4)\) (which is the same group as \(SO(6)\), at least locally), and the subgroup that leaves one such spinor alone is \(SU(3)\). Compact, Ricci flat manifolds of this type with holonomy \(SU(3)\) are called Calabi-Yau manifolds. Calabi conjectured in the 1950s that they exist, and Yau proved it in 1977, decades before anyone suspected they had anything to do with physics.
Now for the punchline. In the heterotic string, Candelas, Horowitz, Strominger and Witten showed in 1985 that the simplest choice is to set the gauge connection on \(X\) equal to the spin connection, so the gauge curvature literally is the Riemann curvature of the hidden space, and our dictionary becomes an equality. With this choice, the \(E_8\) gauge group of the string is broken to \(E_6\), which is itself a GUT group, and the net number of generations of quarks and leptons is
\[\begin{equation}
N_{\text{gen}} = \frac{1}{2}\left|\chi(X)\right| \, ,
\end{equation}\]
where \(\chi(X)\) is the Euler characteristic of the Calabi-Yau. It can be computed from the six-dimensional version of Gauss-Bonnet, due to Chern,
\[\begin{equation}
\chi(X) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^3}\int_X \operatorname{Pf}(\Omega) \, ,
\end{equation}\]
where \(\Omega\) is the curvature two-form and \(\operatorname{Pf}\) is the Pfaffian (a sort of square root of the determinant for antisymmetric matrices). The most famous Calabi-Yau, the quintic, has \(\chi = -200\) and therefore predicts \(100\) generations, which is rather too many. The Tian-Yau manifold has \(\chi = -6\), giving exactly three. So one of the great unexplained numbers of the standard model becomes the integral of curvature over a hidden space. I think Gauss would have been quite pleased.
I should temper the excitement a little. There are an enormous number of Calabi-Yau manifolds (hundreds of millions are known from just one construction, and nobody knows whether the list is finite). Their size and shape can also be varied continuously, and each such deformation shows up in four dimensions as a massless scalar field, called a modulus, which we do not observe and so must somehow be given a mass. People have found compactifications with exactly the particle content of the (supersymmetric) standard model, but getting all of the masses and couplings right, and fixing the moduli, is still an open problem. And of course there is not yet any experimental evidence for strings at all. Even so, the fact that the question “how many generations are there?” can be turned into a question about curvature and topology is, to me, one of the most remarkable things in theoretical physics.

title: Curvature, Curvature, Curvature!
text:
Final Thoughts
We started with a circle and asked how quickly its tangent vector turns. From there we went through Euler’s principal curvatures, Gauss’s fundamental forms and his Theorema egregium, and Riemann’s realisation that curvature can be detected from inside a space by parallel transporting a vector around a loop, or equivalently by the failure of covariant derivatives to commute. That single commutator then gave us Einstein’s gravity, the field strengths of the standard model and, beyond it, Kaluza-Klein theory, monopoles, axions and the shape of hidden dimensions.
If there is one lesson to take away, it is the one I hinted at right back in the section on parameterisation invariance. Coordinates, parameters and gauges are all just labels, which we are free to choose however makes our lives easiest. The physics lives in the things that do not care about these choices: curvature, holonomy, and the integers that come from integrating curvature over closed spaces. It is no coincidence that so many attempts to go beyond the standard model start by asking a geometric question.
What we still do not have is a theory in which gravity and gauge theory are truly on the same footing at the quantum level. Their geometry is almost identical, but their dynamics are not, and that gap is where much of the most exciting work in theoretical physics is happening today.
If you made it this far, thank you (and well done). I hope you now see curvature the way I do: as one of the deepest and most useful ideas we have.

title: Curvature, Curvature, Curvature!
text:
Further Reading
If you want to go further, here are some sources I like.

M. P. do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces. A great place to learn the classical material on curves, surfaces and Gauss-Bonnet properly.
S. Carroll, Spacetime and Geometry: An Introduction to General Relativity. A very readable introduction to Riemannian geometry and general relativity.
M. Nakahara, Geometry, Topology and Physics. The standard reference for connections, fibre bundles, characteristic classes and their uses in physics.
T. Eguchi, P. B. Gilkey and A. J. Hanson, “Gravitation, Gauge Theories and Differential Geometry”, Physics Reports 66 (1980). A classic review of the dictionary between gravity and gauge theory.
D. Tong, Lectures on Gauge Theory (University of Cambridge). Excellent on instantons, monopoles and the \(\theta\) angle.
E. Witten, “Search for a Realistic Kaluza-Klein Theory”, Nuclear Physics B 186 (1981).
P. Candelas, G. T. Horowitz, A. Strominger and E. Witten, “Vacuum Configurations for Superstrings”, Nuclear Physics B 258 (1985).

text: Who doesn’t love a good (ice-cold) beer? I certainly do, and if you have ever wondered if there is a mathematical way to describe the foam from pouring a beer, then you have come to right place. Towards the end I will discuss the surprisingly deep overlap with integrable systems - systems which are exactly solvable, by which we mean we can integrate them to attain a solution.

title: Percentage of Users Attended a Contest
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Percentage of Users Attended a Contest
text:
Problem
Users lists every user; Register records which user registered for which contest (contest_id, user_id). For each contest, report the percentage of all users who registered for it, rounded to two decimal places. Order by percentage (highest first), breaking ties by contest_id (lowest first).

title: Percentage of Users Attended a Contest
text:
Formalisation
Let \(U\) be the set of users and \(R\) the set of registrations. Grouping by contest partitions \(R\) into the classes
\[
R_c = \{\, r \in R \mid r.\mathrm{contest} = c \,\},
\]
and the quantity we want is
\[
p(c) = 100 \cdot \frac{|R_c|}{|U|}.
\]
The numerator depends on the group; the denominator does not. \(|U|\) is one constant for the whole query, so it comes from a separate scalar subquery. Summing over the groups would give the wrong quantity:
\[
\sum_c |R_c| = |R| \neq |U|,
\]
which counts user–contest registrations, not users.
The output is then the sequence of pairs \((c, p(c))\) sorted lexicographically by the key \((-p(c),\ c)\): percentage descending, contest id ascending.

title: Percentage of Users Attended a Contest
text:
Solution
SELECT r.contest_id,
       ROUND(100 * COUNT(r.user_id) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Users), 2)
         AS percentage
FROM Register r
GROUP BY r.contest_id
ORDER BY percentage DESC, r.contest_id ASC;
My working version kept a left join from Users and filtered it:
SELECT r.contest_id,
       ROUND(100 * COUNT(r.contest_id) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Users), 2)
         AS percentage
FROM Users u
LEFT JOIN Register r ON u.user_id = r.user_id
WHERE r.contest_id IS NOT NULL
GROUP BY r.contest_id
ORDER BY percentage DESC, r.contest_id ASC;
It gives the same answer, but the WHERE removes exactly the rows the left join added, leaving an inner join. Since every registration belongs to an existing user, that is just Register, so the join can go.

title: Percentage of Users Attended a Contest
text:
Pitfalls

Aggregates cannot be nested. SUM(COUNT(...)) is rejected in a grouped query. A constant that is the same for every group belongs in a scalar subquery: (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Users).
A left join from Users creates a NULL group. Users who registered for nothing get a row with contest_id NULL, which GROUP BY turns into a spurious “NULL contest”.
Clauses have a fixed written order: SELECT → FROM → JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → ORDER BY. I first wrote WHERE before FROM.
!= 'NULL' only works by accident. MySQL casts the string 'NULL' to 0, so the test becomes contest_id != 0, and NULL != 0 is UNKNOWN, which WHERE drops. The correct test is IS NOT NULL.
A WHERE condition on the right-hand table cancels a LEFT JOIN. The same rule as in 1251, here used on purpose, which is the sign the join is unnecessary.
COUNT(*) counts rows; COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values. After a left join they differ on the padded rows.
ORDER BY can use the SELECT alias (ORDER BY percentage), because ORDER BY runs after SELECT.

title: Project Employees I
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Project Employees I
text:
Problem
Project records which employees work on which project (project_id, employee_id); Employee gives each employee’s name and experience_years. For each project, report the average experience of its employees, rounded to two decimal places.

title: Project Employees I
text:
Formalisation
Let \(P\) be the project table and \(E\) the employee table, and let \(f : P \to I\) and \(g : E \to I\) read off the employee id. The join is the fibre product (pullback) of \(P \xrightarrow{f} I \xleftarrow{g} E\):
\[
P \times_I E = \{(p, e) \in P \times E \mid f(p) = g(e)\}.
\]
Written with ON, SQL keeps every coordinate of both factors, giving 5-tuples \((\mathrm{pid}, \mathrm{eid}, \mathrm{eid}', \mathrm{name}, \mathrm{exp})\) with \(\mathrm{eid} = \mathrm{eid}'\). Projecting out the redundant coordinate is a bijection onto the “glued” 4-tuples, which is what JOIN ... USING (employee_id) returns.
The fibre product is taken fibre by fibre, \((P \times_I E)_i = f^{-1}(i) \times g^{-1}(i)\), so its size is
\[
|P \times_I E| = \sum_{i \in I} |f^{-1}(i)|\,|g^{-1}(i)|.
\]
Since employee_id is the key of Employee, every \(|g^{-1}(i)| \le 1\): the join attaches an employee to each project row and never multiplies rows.
Grouping by project then partitions the joined set into the classes \(E_j = \{(p,e) \mid p.\mathrm{pid} = j\}\), and the answer is the mean over each class:
\[
\bar x_j = \frac{1}{|E_j|} \sum_{(p,e) \in E_j} e.\mathrm{exp}.
\]

title: Project Employees I
text:
Solution
SELECT p.project_id,
  ROUND(AVG(e.experience_years), 2) AS average_years
FROM Project p
JOIN Employee e ON p.employee_id = e.employee_id
GROUP BY p.project_id;

title: Project Employees I
text:
Pitfalls

ON keeps both id columns; USING merges them. SELECT * on an ON join shows employee_id twice. Harmless for an inner join, but after a LEFT JOIN the two columns differ (one can be NULL), so choose which one to select.
Check the key before trusting an aggregate. The row-count formula above is why this AVG is correct: each project row matches at most one employee. Join on a non-key column and rows multiply, which reweights AVG and inflates SUM without any error.
An inner join is enough here. Every employee_id in Project exists in Employee, and projects with no employees never appear in Project, so no rows need to be kept with NULL padding.

title: Triangle Judgement
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Triangle Judgement
text:
Problem
Each row of Triangle holds three positive lengths x, y, z. For every row, report whether the three segments can form a triangle ('Yes' or 'No').

title: Triangle Judgement
text:
Formalisation
This is not a selection: every row is kept. Instead each tuple is extended by a computed value, a generalised projection
\[
\pi_{\,x,\,y,\,z,\,\chi(x,y,z)}(T), \qquad
\chi(x,y,z) =
\begin{cases}
\text{Yes}, & x + y > z \ \wedge\ x + z > y \ \wedge\ y + z > x, \\
\text{No}, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]
The three inequalities collapse to one. Without loss of generality let \(z = \max(x,y,z)\). Then \(x + z > z \ge y\) and \(y + z > z \ge x\) (all lengths are positive), so the second and third inequalities hold automatically and only \(x + y > z\) can fail. Hence
\[
\chi(x,y,z) = \text{Yes} \iff x + y + z > 2\max(x,y,z).
\]
This also explains my first attempt: testing only \(x + y > z\) is correct exactly when \(z\) happens to be the longest side.

title: Triangle Judgement
text:
Solution
SELECT x, y, z,
  CASE
    WHEN x + y > z AND x + z > y AND y + z > x THEN 'Yes'
    ELSE 'No'
  END AS triangle
FROM Triangle;
The single-test version from the formalisation:
SELECT x, y, z,
  CASE WHEN x + y + z > 2 * GREATEST(x, y, z) THEN 'Yes' ELSE 'No' END AS triangle
FROM Triangle;

title: Triangle Judgement
text:
Pitfalls

Check all three inequalities, not one. My first version treated z as the special side and tested only x + y <= z, which passes whenever z is the longest side and fails otherwise (8 of 11 tests passed).
The inequality is strict. If \(x + y = z\) the “triangle” is flat (degenerate), so the answer is 'No'.
ABS is unnecessary. The values are lengths, so they are positive.
GREATEST is not MAX. GREATEST(x, y, z) takes the largest of several values in one row; MAX(col) is an aggregate over many rows.
CASE builds a column; WHERE removes rows. Here every row must appear in the output, so the condition goes in a CASE, not a WHERE.

title: Average Selling Price
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Average Selling Price
text:
Problem
Prices gives each product’s price over date ranges (start_date to end_date); UnitsSold records sales (product_id, purchase_date, units). For every product, report the average selling price, weighted by units sold and rounded to two decimal places, or 0 if the product never sold.

title: Average Selling Price
text:
Formalisation
For product \(j\), pair each sale \(k\) with the price in force on its purchase date, giving pairs \((p_k, u_k)\) of price and units. The answer is the units-weighted mean
\[
\bar p_j = \frac{\sum_k p_k\, u_k}{\sum_k u_k},
\]
with \(\bar p_j = 0\) when product \(j\) has no sales (where both sums are empty). Note that \(\bar p_j \neq \frac{1}{n}\sum_k p_k\): averaging the prices would ignore how many units sold at each one.

title: Average Selling Price
text:
Solution
SELECT p.product_id,
       IFNULL(ROUND(SUM(p.price * u.units) / SUM(u.units), 2), 0)
         AS average_price
FROM Prices p
LEFT JOIN UnitsSold u
  ON p.product_id = u.product_id
 AND u.purchase_date BETWEEN p.start_date AND p.end_date
GROUP BY p.product_id;

title: Average Selling Price
text:
Pitfalls
My attempt had the right structure but two bugs:

a <= b <= c does not mean what it does in maths. SQL evaluates it as (a <= b) <= c: the first comparison returns 1 or 0, which is then compared with a date. Write b BETWEEN a AND c (inclusive at both ends) or a <= b AND b <= c.
A condition on the right-hand table in WHERE turns a LEFT JOIN into an inner join. For a product with no sales, u.purchase_date is NULL, every comparison with it is UNKNOWN, and WHERE discards the row. Conditions in ON decide how rows pair up; conditions in WHERE remove rows afterwards.
Join on the date range, not just product_id. Joining on product_id alone pairs every sale with every price period and inflates the totals.
No sales means both sums are NULL. IFNULL(..., 0) turns the result into the required 0.

title: Rising Temperature
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Rising Temperature
text:
Problem
Weather records a temperature for each recordDate (one row per date, but some dates may be missing). Return the id of every day that was warmer than the previous calendar day.

title: Rising Temperature
text:
Formalisation
A self-join pairs the table with itself, so we need two independent variables ranging over the same set \(W\):
\[
\{\, w.\mathrm{id} \mid w, w' \in W,\ w'.\mathrm{date} = w.\mathrm{date} - 1\ \text{day},\ w.\mathrm{temp} > w'.\mathrm{temp} \,\}.
\]
Days whose previous date is missing have no partner \(w'\) and so drop out, which is what we want.

title: Rising Temperature
text:
Solution
SELECT today.id
FROM Weather today
JOIN Weather yesterday
  ON yesterday.recordDate = DATE_SUB(today.recordDate, INTERVAL 1 DAY)
WHERE today.temperature > yesterday.temperature;
A window-function version works too, but only if it checks the gap explicitly:
WITH w AS (
  SELECT id, recordDate, temperature,
         LAG(recordDate)  OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_date,
         LAG(temperature) OVER (ORDER BY recordDate) AS prev_temp
  FROM Weather
)
SELECT id FROM w
WHERE DATEDIFF(recordDate, prev_date) = 1
  AND temperature > prev_temp;

title: Rising Temperature
text:
Pitfalls

date - 1 is not date arithmetic in MySQL. It converts '2024-03-01' to the number 20240301 and subtracts 1, which breaks at every month boundary. Use DATE_SUB(d, INTERVAL 1 DAY) or DATEDIFF(a, b).
LAG gives the previous row, not the previous day. If a date is missing, LAG compares with an older day instead. That is the trap in this problem.

title: Not Boring Movies
text: Problem on LeetCode

title: Not Boring Movies
text:
Problem
Cinema lists movies with an id, a name, a description and a rating. Report the movies with an odd id whose description is not 'boring', ordered by rating from highest to lowest.

title: Not Boring Movies
text:
Formalisation
Let \(C \subseteq \mathbb{N} \times M \times D \times \mathbb{R}\) be the table, with tuples \((i, m, d, r)\). First filter, then project:
\[
\pi_{i,m,d,r}\big(\sigma_{\,i \equiv 1 \ (\mathrm{mod}\ 2)\ \wedge\ d \neq \text{boring}}(C)\big) = \{(i,m,d,r) \in C \mid i \text{ odd},\ d \neq \text{boring}\}.
\]
The projection keeps every column, so here it is the identity and the answer is just the selection.
The ordering is not part of the algebra: a relation is an unordered set, so ORDER BY turns the result into a sequence \((t_1, t_2, \dots)\) with \(t_k.r \ge t_{k+1}.r\). That is why ordering always comes last, after the set has been built.

title: Not Boring Movies
text:
Solution
SELECT c.id, c.movie, c.description, c.rating
FROM Cinema c
WHERE c.id % 2 != 0 AND c.description != 'boring'
ORDER BY c.rating DESC;

title: Not Boring Movies
text:
Pitfalls

Order by the column the question asks for. My first version used ORDER BY c.id DESC, which passes the example only by coincidence: there, ids 5 and 1 have ratings 9.1 and 8.9, so both orderings agree.
!= 0 is safer than = 1 for odd numbers. In MySQL, -3 % 2 = -1, so id % 2 = 1 would miss negative odd ids. Ids here are positive, but the habit is worth keeping. MOD(id, 2) behaves the same way.
!= drops NULLs. If a description were NULL, description != 'boring' would be UNKNOWN and WHERE would discard the row, even though a missing description is not “boring”. To keep such rows, write (description != 'boring' OR description IS NULL).
